zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical checkpoint after independent scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Supplied page subset used for headword coverage only; diplomatic readings and commentary are this review's own. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Continues Yaneuo macuru from f300: removing the roof covering. The new example Vdeuo macuru concerns rolling clothing back from the arms; the initial Deſtelhar is body text here, although it also appeared as the preceding page's catchword.
Arregaçar os braços translates rolling up at the arms. The next example contrasts pursuit and being driven back in fighting, and continues with tatacǒ below.

runs.text: Pelejar ora leuando diante o inimi-

lines.note: Tatacǒ completes the fighting example. The translation begins fighting while at one moment driving the enemy ahead; inimi- continues as inimigo.
Go completes inimigo, and the alternative is falling back. Faritçuqe then introduces the pasted-paper object of another macuru example.

runs.text: Tirar o papel que eſta pe-

lines.note: Xǒji is offered as an alternative to faritçuqe. Here macuru means stripping off the paper, with pe- beginning Portuguese pegado.

runs.text: gado na parede, ou nas portas de papel. ¶

lines.note: The paper is attached to the wall or to paper doors. Nin begins the next Japanese example across the physical line break; no missing hyphen is supplied.
Ninjuuo macuritatçuru concerns driving people before oneself. The Portuguese begins the same explanation, dividing gente after gẽ-.
Te completes gente: driving people ahead in fighting or an encounter. A further Ninjuuo example starts here and divides macuri after ma-.

runs.text: Leuar diante deſi, ou fazer ſu-

lines.note: Macuri aguru describes driving people ahead or making them go upward. The printed internal word gap is retained; the Portuguese verb subir continues below. The small worn terminal mark after ſu is retained as the aligned draft’s hyphen, but its exact shape remains uncertain.
Bir completes subir. The people are driven up a hill or mountain, completing the preceding directional example.
Macuri idaxi is driving or casting something out forcefully. The principal part aita is the historical inflection of the s-stem, not a spelling to modernize.
The example says that the enemies who had been inside were driven out. The visibly doubled t in Ittaru is retained, rather than silently regularized from the interpretation.

runs.text: os inimigos fora que eſtauão dentro.

lines.note: Os inimigos fora que eſtauão dentro completes the expulsion example: enemies formerly within are put outside.
Macuriſague is driving something downward. Only uru is printed as an additional principal form here; no missing past form is reconstructed.

Ninjuuo macuri ſaguru illustrates driving people down, followed by alternative verbs. Vo- begins voroſu below; this isolated final fragment is visibly italic, unlike the preceding upright Japanese example and the continuation on the next row.
Voroſu and votoſu are further downward-motion alternatives. The Portuguese then begins explaining driving the people ahead and throwing them down; de- continues as deitala.
Itala completes deitala: casting the people downward or overthrowing them. The printed a baixo remains separate words.

runs.text: Grãos que comem os caualos. Vt,

lines.note: Macuſa is horse fodder, described here as grain eaten by horses. The definition, rather than a modern plant classification, determines the interpretation.

runs.text: Dar grãos a comer aos caualos.

lines.note: Macuſauo cǒ means feeding the horses. The Portuguese phrase is a comer aos caualos; the OCR incorrectly divided it as comera os.

runs.text: Hũa erua que folgão os caualos de

lines.note: Macuzu names a plant horses enjoy eating. The description continues with a comparison rather than an exact botanical identification.
Comer completes the feeding description. Era is the printed historical ivy-name used for the comparison, not an editorial heading or a Japanese synonym.

runs.text: Lugar onde ha muita deſta erua.

lines.note: Macuzuvara denotes a place where much of the preceding plant grows. Deſta erua refers directly back to Macuzu.
Macuzucuxi redirects to Macuguxi, the curtain-supporting poles on f300. Vide is italic apparatus; the cited Japanese headword remains upright within the cross-reference.
Mada means not yet when used with negative verbs. The scan reads verbos, not OCR verbas; this distinction is grammatical, not a definition of negative words in general.
Conoguiuo mada itaſazu illustrates not yet having done this matter. Mon. is an upright citation label; A- begins the Portuguese Ainda across the break.

runs.text: inda não fiz iſto. ¶ Item, Ainda cõ ver

lines.note: The example is translated as not yet having done this. The visible gap in fiz iſto is restored. A second use begins: ainda with affirmative verbs, whose name continues without a printed hyphen after ver.
Bos completes verbos, and affirmatiuos corrects the OCR l to visible t. Saqeua mada aruca asks whether wine still remains, illustrating positive still rather than negative not yet.
Hà ainda vinho? is the Portuguese question corresponding to the preceding Japanese example. The final mark is a question mark, not the OCR nasalized vowel ẽ.
Madaqi is labelled poetic and glossed as something hurried or early. P. introduces the explanation and retains the supplied italic setting.
Madara means mottled or marked, compared here with a tiger or cat. The following examples develop the same colour-pattern sense.
Madara inu is a dog with patches of different colours. Diuerſas leads into cores on the following row.
Cores completes the dog example. Fara madarano gan introduces a wild waterbird with a marked underside; the Portuguese calls it pato, so no modern zoological identification is imposed.

runs.text: brauo q̃ tẽ os peitos malhados de brãco e preto.

lines.note: Completes the wild-bird description: the breast is mottled white and black. The scan supports malhados and brãco, correcting OCR malbados and brãto; the nasal abbreviation is retained.

runs.text: O abrir, & fechar o olho, ou pes-

lines.note: Madataqi is the opening and closing of the eye, or blinking. The alternative Portuguese verb divides after pes-; its short s is retained rather than changed to long ſ.
Tenejar completes pestenejar. Madataqino aida, alternatively ma, expresses the interval of a blink; the Portuguese interpretation follows below.
The interval is translated as a very brief space of time. Breuißimo has no additional t after ß. Madataqiuo begins the next verbal example.
Suru completes Madataqiuo ſuru: to blink. The compact example and its translation remain on this separate physical row.

runs.text: Ate: vſaſe com algũa outra compoſi-

lines.note: Made expresses a limit, up to or until. The colon after Ate introduces its use in combination with another expression; compoſi- continues on the next line.
Ção completes compoſição. Coremade ſanjita illustrates having come as far as here; the printed Portuguese atequi is retained as one historical word.

runs.text: Ate. Tẽ eſtes modos, & outros ſeme

lines.note: Mademo is introduced through the same up-to sense, with the following idioms showing its extended uses. Seme continues into ſemelhantes without a visible terminal hyphen.
Lhãtes completes the reference to similar ways of speaking. Soremademo gozaranu is the first idiomatic example, translated below in terms of lack of necessity.
Ißo não he neceßario gives the preceding idiom as that is unnecessary. The next example is Qiqumademo, with the narrow dotted i rather than the OCR u, and continues across go-/zanai.
Zanai completes the negative predicate: it is unnecessary to hear. Mairuma- begins the parallel example about going, not a separate entry.
Demo nai completes Mairumademo nai: there is no need to go. The supplied double-long-ſ spelling in neceſſario is retained, not harmonized with the preceding ß forms.
Mado is a window, glossed by historical Portuguese Ianella. It is distinct from the following long-vowel Madǒ.
Madǒ is paraphrased as Tenguno michi. The Portuguese renders this as the devil’s path; this records the dictionary’s religious interpretation, not an identification adopted independently here.
Madoi denotes wandering or being mistaken. Cocoromadô applies the same idea to mental confusion; the printed circumflexes are preserved separately from the preceding headword’s caron.

runs.text: Não eſtar ẽ ſi, ou eſtar muito perturbado.

lines.note: The mental-state example means not being oneself, or being greatly disturbed. Perturbado is one printed word; the OCR’s internal space is removed.

Madoi ariqi is wandering about, with error or aimlessness emphasized by the gloss. The unusual Portuguese expression begins a- and continues as nhoto; it is not silently replaced with a modern equivalent.
Nhoto completes the preceding printed expression, followed by hither and thither. The scan shows a grave accent in decà as well as là; the first pair remains tightly joined as decà.
Madoromi denotes dozing or sleeping lightly. The three principal forms retain the circumflex in ôda; a cited example starts on the next row.

The example says that the storm was so fierce that even dozing was impossible. Chosen Araxiga restores a severely under-inked r after A: only a faint remnant survives, but its position, the remaining axiga, and the wind translation support this reading. Cotomo has worn bowls, not grounds for changing its vowel letters.

Naqereba completes the negative clause. Feiq. is the upright source label, followed by italic Lib. i.; the Portuguese begins with the strong wind, dividing vento after vẽ-. The comma after naqereba and the italic &c. are retained from the scan.

runs.text: to rijo não auiapoder repouſar, nem dormir

lines.note: To completes vento: the wind was strong, preventing repose or sleep. The tightly set auiapoder is interpreted as auia poder, but the supplied joined spacing is retained because an independent word space is not secure.
Hum pouco completes the translation: not even a little rest or sleep was possible. This short continuation is body text, not a new definition.
Madouaxi is the causative, making someone lose the way or go wrong. Cami- starts caminho, whose literal and religious applications continue below.

runs.text: nho. ¶ Item, Enganar, ou fazer errar

lines.note: Nho completes caminho. The paragraph then adds deception or causing another person to err, leading into the specifically religious path below.
The extended sense is making someone err on the path of salvation. This is the dictionary’s explanatory frame for the causative, not a separate Japanese example.
Madouo is paraphrased by Aida touoi: a long interval or distance. The historical Japanese spelling touoi is retained, and the Portuguese definition continues onto the next row.
Distancia completes the spatial definition. Its locally supplied st spelling is retained without attempting a systematic reclassification of the italic ligature.

Madouoni is the adverbial form, at a distance. The initial is visibly M, not OCR N. The chosen gloss Longe, ou em distancia repairs severe under-inking: the g descender, remnants of ou em, and the ending of distancia remain, while the immediately preceding definition supplies a same-typeface lexical comparator. Several intervening strokes remain uncertain.

Mafitotçu means one more. Reinspection prompted by the attributed NINJAL checkpoint shows a damaged a followed directly by the fi types, not the draft’s extra i in Maifitotçu; the surviving spacing and letter count support the correction.
Mafô is paraphrased as Tenguno nori, rendered as the devil’s law. The circumflex distinguishes the printed form from adjacent words with other vowel marks.

Mafôxa denotes a practitioner associated in the gloss with superstitions, divination, and further rites continued below. The characterization belongs to the historical dictionary’s religious vocabulary; the printed Portuguese list is not rewritten to regularize its grammar.
Completes the practitioner’s description with other ceremonies attributed to the devil. The scan reads do without the OCR tilde.
Mafǔ names a wind attributed to the devil. The caron over u is copied as a mark of the print, not converted to the adjacent headwords’ circumflex.
Mafuſagui is the cover of a quiver. The scan reads aljaua without an extra ſ; the initial Ç of Çapadoura has a visible cedilla and is retained despite the tempting unaccented C.
Magai denotes error, confusion, or doubt. Magaimo- begins an example denying any doubt, completed by nai below.
Nai completes Magaimo nai: there is nothing to doubt. The Portuguese repeats that sense explicitly.
The verb Magai is glossed as erring or doubting. Both principal-form vowel marks are carons; Su- begins the following example rather than a new headword.
Sucoximo magauanu introduces something not in the least doubtful: Joseph’s clothing. The European name Ioſephga is written as part of the upright Japanese example and the predicate divides na-/rito.

runs.text: Gos. He a tunica de Ioſeph ſem

lines.note: Rito completes the assertion that it is Joseph’s tunic. The reference 2. p. is upright, while Gos. has the slanted setting visible in the scan. The translation continues after ſem onto an omitted physical row restored below; no words are appended artificially to this row.

Completes ſem duuida algũa: without any doubt. This real physical row was omitted by the provisional OCR; the scan shows the abbreviation tilde over u in algũa, and the sentence ends here before Magaqi.

Magaqi is labelled poetic and explained by Chijſai caqi, a small enclosure or hedge. The scan has P. rather than B., and the explanatory i. is separately set; no later lines are renumbered after the restored continuation above.

runs.text: ou diuiſão de canas, &c. que ſe faz nas Ni-

lines.note: The hedge may be a division made of canes. Ni- is the first part of the Japanese garden-name embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not part of an independent Japanese example.
Uas completes Niuas, glossed by alegretes, garden plots. The pluralized Japanese borrowing belongs inside the Portuguese sentence and retains the italic setting visible here.
Magari means becoming bent or crooked. The paragraph introduces a metaphorical use; the principal form atta retains its double t.
Cocorono magatta fito describes a person whose heart is crooked, translated as deceitful or false. Refalſado is retained as printed rather than modernized.
Magaſumi, equated with Mayori, is discharge or crust at the eyes. Mayori is a Japanese synonym after i, not a Portuguese word or a typeface-toggle term.
Mago means a grandchild, rendered by masculine Portuguese Neto. This short line is an independent headword entry.
Mague is equated with Maxǒ and Tenguno ſamatague, an obstruction attributed to a devil or tengu. The Portuguese equivalent is divided Es-/toruo; the short s is retained.
Toruo completes Estoruo, obstruction, qualified as of the devil. This short continuation belongs to the nominal Mague entry above, not the inflected verb below.
The verb Mague means bending or curving something. Uru and eta are its principal-form endings, contrasting with intransitive Magari above.
The metaphorical example Riuo fini maguru is bending what is right into what is wrong. Dobrar begins the Portuguese explanation on this row.

runs.text: a rezão à ſem rezão, ou injuſtiça. Vt,

lines.note: The metaphor is translated as bending reason or justice toward unreason or injustice. Both occurrences of rezão retain their historical e spelling; Cu- begins a further comparison involving a cart.
Cu-/rumaua gives the cart topic, followed by a statement about not pushing it sideways. Riua introduces the parallel topic of reason; ma- divides the verb maguete.
Guete completes maguete in the comparison about distorting reason. Xix. is an upright citation label, followed by the Portuguese translation beginning Aßi co-.

runs.text: mo o carro não pode ir torto, aßi torcendo a-

lines.note: Mo completes como: just as a cart cannot go crookedly, so twisting reason has the consequence below. The scan has a real space in pode ir; the short printed mark after the final a is retained rather than inferred merely from continuation.
The translation concludes that reason is not understood when distorted. The scan reads rezão, with e, not the draft’s razão; the split after the preceding article a- is kept as physical typography.

Maguiracaxi concerns confusing or mixing things up. The scan prints u, not the morphologically expected ſu, so no consonant is supplied; the following examples identify the s-stem. A faint but separate period follows Emburulhar. The crop is extended upward to include the complete initial M.

runs.text: vezes ſe compoem com as raizes de muitos

lines.note: The usage note says that the verb is sometimes compounded with the roots of many verbs. This Portuguese grammatical explanation continues through verbos on the next physical row.
Torimaguiracaſu is the first compound example. Its translation begins tomar, taking, with the object and mistaken substitution supplied below.
The first compound means taking one thing for another. Mimaguiracaſu then introduces the corresponding visual confusion, remaining upright Japanese rather than part of the italic translation.
Mimaguiracaſu is translated as seeing one thing as another. Qiqimagui- begins the hearing counterpart; its narrow first i is weakly inked but not replaced by a space or another vowel.
Racaſu completes Qiqimaguiracaſu, hearing one thing as another. The entry ends with &c.; the isolated Magui- below the column is a separate catchword, not additional body text.
